o:
Normalize each address: local part loses dots, everything from the first '+' onward, and is lowercased; domain is lowercased. Group count = number of distinct normalized local@domain pairs. With ≤ 1000 short emails, a hash set of normalized keys solves it directly.

Example 1 yields two distinct keys (differing domains). Example 2 shows '+' truncation ('ab+xy' → 'ab') and case folding ('A'/'a'). Example 3 collapses all three to ab@domain.com.
k: Normalization is purely mechanical; a set of canonical keys counts the groups.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash set of normalized keys
a.i: Split at '@', apply the local rules (cut at '+', strip '.', lowercase), lowercase the domain, insert local+'@'+domain into a set, return its size.
s: For each email, split into local and domain at '@'.
Insert the composed key into a set; return the set size.
a.t: O(total input length) — each character is processed a constant number of times
a.sp: O(total input length) — the set of keys

a.n: Approach 2: Sort normalized keys and count distinct
a.i: Build all normalized keys into an array, sort it, and count positions where the key differs from its predecessor. Avoids hashing; useful in environments where hash sets are disallowed, at the cost of an extra log factor.
s: Normalize every email into a key array.
Count indices i where key[i] != key[i-1] (plus 1 if non-empty).
a.t: O(N log N) where N is total input length — sorting the keys dominates

w: Use the hash-set version. Pitfalls: stripping dots after '+' truncation is moot (everything after '+' is dropped anyway), and forgetting the domain lowercase. Note this differs from classic LeetCode 929 only in that the domain is also normalized. Follow-up: return the groups themselves rather than the count (group by key into a map).
